claim: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is generated through phosphorylation of sphingosine by sphingosine kinases (Sphk1 and Sphk2).
source: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is generated through phosphorylation of sphingosine by sphingosine kinases (Sphk1 and Sphk2).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about S1P biosynthesis.

claim: sphk2 maternal-zygotic mutant zebrafish embryos (sphk2MZ) display a delay in epiboly.
source: We show that sphk2 maternal-zygotic mutant zebrafish embryos (sphk2MZ) display early developmental phenotypes, including a delay in epiboly, depleted S1P levels, elevated levels of sphingosine, and resistance to sphingosine toxicity.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental observations of sphk2MZ embryos showing delayed epiboly.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos have depleted S1P levels.
source: We show that sphk2 maternal-zygotic mutant zebrafish embryos (sphk2MZ) display early developmental phenotypes, including a delay in epiboly, depleted S1P levels, elevated levels of sphingosine, and resistance to sphingosine toxicity.
evidence: Lipidomic profiling data presented in the manuscript confirms depleted S1P levels.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos have elevated levels of sphingosine.
source: We show that sphk2 maternal-zygotic mutant zebrafish embryos (sphk2MZ) display early developmental phenotypes, including a delay in epiboly, depleted S1P levels, elevated levels of sphingosine, and resistance to sphingosine toxicity.
evidence: Lipidomic profiling data presented in the manuscript shows elevated sphingosine levels.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos show resistance to sphingosine toxicity.
source: We show that sphk2 maternal-zygotic mutant zebrafish embryos (sphk2MZ) display early developmental phenotypes, including a delay in epiboly, depleted S1P levels, elevated levels of sphingosine, and resistance to sphingosine toxicity.
evidence: Experimental data shows sphk2MZ embryos tolerate exogenous sphingosine treatment better than wildtype.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos have strikingly increased levels of maternal transcripts encoding ceramide synthase 2b (Cers2b).
source: The sphk2MZ embryos also have strikingly increased levels of maternal transcripts encoding ceramide synthase 2b (Cers2b), and loss of Cers2b in sphk2MZ embryos phenocopies sphingosine toxicity.
evidence: qRT-PCR data shows significant upregulation of cers2b transcripts in sphk2MZ embryos.

claim: Loss of Cers2b in sphk2MZ embryos phenocopies sphingosine toxicity.
source: The sphk2MZ embryos also have strikingly increased levels of maternal transcripts encoding ceramide synthase 2b (Cers2b), and loss of Cers2b in sphk2MZ embryos phenocopies sphingosine toxicity.
evidence: Morpholino knockdown and genetic interaction experiments show that loss of Cers2b causes gastrulation defects in sphk2MZ embryos.

claim: An upstream region of the cers2b promoter supports enhanced expression of a reporter gene in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype embryos.
source: An upstream region of the cers2b promoter supports enhanced expression of a reporter gene in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype embryos.
evidence: Luciferase reporter assays show 9-fold higher activity in sphk2MZ embryos.

claim: Ectopic expression of Cers2b protein reduces activity of the cers2b promoter.
source: Furthermore, ectopic expression of Cers2b protein itself reduces activity of the promoter, and this repression is relieved by exogenous sphingosine.
evidence: Luciferase reporter assays in HEK293T cells show Cers2b represses its own promoter.

claim: Cers2b-mediated repression of the cers2b promoter is relieved by exogenous sphingosine.
source: Furthermore, ectopic expression of Cers2b protein itself reduces activity of the promoter, and this repression is relieved by exogenous sphingosine.
evidence: Luciferase reporter assays show sphingosine treatment relieves Cers2b repression.

claim: The sphk2MZ genome recognizes the lack of sphingosine kinase activity and up-regulates cers2b as a salvage pathway for sphingosine turnover.
source: Therefore, the sphk2MZ genome recognizes the lack of sphingosine kinase activity and up-regulates cers2b as a salvage pathway for sphingosine turnover.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing cers2b upregulation in sphk2MZ embryos.

claim: Cers2b can function as a sphingolipid-responsive factor to mediate at least part of a feedback regulatory mechanism.
source: Cers2b can also function as a sphingolipid-responsive factor to mediate at least part of a feedback regulatory mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing Cers2b can regulate its own promoter in a sphingosine-dependent manner.

claim: S1P signaling plays key roles during embryogenesis, including developmental angiogenesis, cardiogenesis, limb development and neurogenesis.
source: However, S1P signaling also plays key roles during embryogenesis, including developmental angiogenesis, cardiogenesis, limb development and neurogenesis (Proia and Hla, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: S1P binds to five G-protein-coupled receptors (S1P1–5) that are widely-expressed and function either alone or together to regulate various developmental and physiological functions.
source: S1P binds to five G-protein-coupled receptors (S1P1–5) that are widely-expressed and function either alone or together to regulate various developmental and physiological functions (Mendelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: S1P can only be generated via phosphorylation of sphingosine by sphingosine kinase, encoded by two genes (sphk1 and sphk2) that are highly conserved in vertebrates.
source: S1P can only be generated via phosphorylation of sphingosine by sphingosine kinase, encoded by two genes (sphk1 and sphk2) that are highly conserved in vertebrates.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about S1P biosynthesis.

claim: In zebrafish, sphk2 is expressed during the earliest stages of embryogenesis, including as a maternal transcript.
source: In zebrafish, sphk2 is expressed during the earliest stages of embryogenesis, including as a maternal transcript (Mendelson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mouse embryos tolerate knockout of either Sphk1 or Sphk2.
source: Mouse embryos tolerate knockout of either Sphk1 or Sphk2 (Allende et al., 2004), which implies that Sphk1 and Sphk2 function redundantly and can compensate for each other's loss.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sphk1 and Sphk2 function redundantly and can compensate for each other's loss.
source: Mouse embryos tolerate knockout of either Sphk1 or Sphk2 (Allende et al., 2004), which implies that Sphk1 and Sphk2 function redundantly and can compensate for each other's loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that single knockouts are viable.

claim: Global or hematopoietic-specific knockout of both Sphk1 and Sphk2 is embryonic lethal between E11.5–13.5 due to vascular developmental defects.
source: Indeed, global or hematopoietic-specific (erythrocyte and platelet) knockout of both Sphk1 and Sphk2 is embryonic lethal between E11.5–13.5 due to vascular developmental defects (Gazit et al., 2016; Mizugishi et al., 2005; Xiong et al., 2014) that are similar to those observed in mice lacking all three receptors S1P1-3 (Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vascular developmental defects in double Sphk1/Sphk2 knockout mice are similar to those observed in mice lacking all three receptors S1P1-3.
source: Indeed, global or hematopoietic-specific (erythrocyte and platelet) knockout of both Sphk1 and Sphk2 is embryonic lethal between E11.5–13.5 due to vascular developmental defects (Gazit et al., 2016; Mizugishi et al., 2005; Xiong et al., 2014) that are similar to those observed in mice lacking all three receptors S1P1-3 (Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A point mutation in the gene miles apart (mil), which encodes S1P2, prevents cardiac precursor cells from migrating to the midline, resulting in formation of two separate defective hearts or cardia bifida.
source: A point mutation in the gene miles apart (mil), which encodes S1P2, prevents cardiac precursor cells from migrating to the midline, resulting in formation of two separate defective hearts or cardia bifida (Kupperman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mutants two of hearts (toh) and ko157 phenocopy the mil cardiac defect and are caused by recessive mutations in the sphingolipid transporter gene, spinster2 (spns2).
source: The mutants two of hearts (toh) and ko157 phenocopy the mil cardiac defect and are caused by recessive mutations in the sphingolipid transporter gene, spinster2 (spns2) (Kawahara et al., 2009; Osborne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: sphk2 maternal zygotic mutants phenocopy null zygotic mutants of s1pr2 and spns2.
source: We (Mendelson et al., 2015) and others (Hisano et al., 2015a) generated maternal zygotic mutants for sphk2 (sphk2MZ) and showed that these embryos phenocopy null zygotic mutants of s1pr2 and spns2.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos display a subtle but consistent developmental delay during gastrulation, compared to time-matched wildtype embryos, particularly obvious around 7–8 hr post fertilization (hpf).
source: Upon close examination of developing embryos, we noticed that sphk2MZ embryos display a subtle but consistent developmental delay during gastrulation, compared to time-matched wildtype embryos, particularly obvious around 7–8 hr post fertilization (hpf) (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and imaging of embryos shown in Figure 1.

claim: The developmental delay observed in sphk2MZ embryos was recapitulated in wildtype embryos treated with 3 μM sphingosine.
source: The developmental delay observed in sphk2MZ embryos was recapitulated in wildtype embryos treated with 3 μM sphingosine (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is based on experimental treatment of wildtype embryos with sphingosine, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Wildtype embryos were unaffected by culturing in the presence of ceramide (20 μM), S1P (20 μM), or N-acetyl-D-sphingosine (20 μM).
source: In contrast, wildtype embryos were unaffected by culturing in the presence of ceramide (20 μM), S1P (20 μM), or N-acetyl-D-sphingosine (20 μM) (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is based on experimental treatment of wildtype embryos with various sphingolipids, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Quantitative lipidomics profiling confirmed that the mutant embryos are depleted of S1P to essentially undetectable levels.
source: Quantitative lipidomics profiling confirmed that the mutant embryos are depleted of S1P to essentially undetectable levels.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic profiling data presented in Figure 1J.

claim: The mutant embryos have excessive levels of sphingosine and total long chain ceramides.
source: However, this analysis also revealed that the mutant embryos have excessive levels of sphingosine and total long chain ceramides (Figure 1J,K), likely due to substrate backup caused by lack of sphingosine kinase and reverse reactions that form ceramide.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic profiling data presented in Figure 1J,K.

claim: Excessive sphingosine and ceramide levels in mutant embryos are likely due to substrate backup caused by lack of sphingosine kinase and reverse reactions that form ceramide.
source: However, this analysis also revealed that the mutant embryos have excessive levels of sphingosine and total long chain ceramides (Figure 1J,K), likely due to substrate backup caused by lack of sphingosine kinase and reverse reactions that form ceramide.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the observed lipid profiles.

claim: In the absence of Sphk2, embryos accumulate excessive levels of the precursor substrate sphingosine, associated with a developmental delay during gastrulation.
source: These observations indicate that in the absence of Sphk2, embryos accumulate excessive levels of the precursor substrate sphingosine, associated with a developmental delay during gastrulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing sphingosine accumulation and developmental delay.

claim: Treatment of wildtype embryos with 5 μM D-erythro-sphingosine (the active naturally occurring isomer) or 5 μM L-erythro-sphingosine (an inactive isomer) caused developmental collapse during epiboly.
source: Treatment of wildtype embryos with 5 μM D-erythro-sphingosine (the active naturally occurring isomer) or 5 μM L-erythro-sphingosine (an inactive isomer) caused developmental collapse during epiboly, a stage of collective cell migration of epiblast cells during gastrulation.
evidence: This is based on experimental treatment of wildtype embryos shown in Figure 2.

claim: At around 50–60% epiboly, in 100% of the treated embryos, epiboly arrests, the epiblast pinches off the yolk cell, and the yolk membrane ruptures, leading to embryonic lethality.
source: At around 50–60% epiboly, in 100% of the treated embryos, epiboly arrests, the epiblast pinches off the yolk cell, and the yolk membrane ruptures, leading to embryonic lethality (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Treatment with sphingosine analogues (psychosine, dimethylsphingosine, and safingol) recapitulated the epiboly phenotype.
source: Treatment with sphingosine analogues (psychosine, dimethylsphingosine, and safingol) recapitulated this epiboly phenotype (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental treatment with sphingosine analogues shown in Figure 2.

claim: Treatment with two chemical inhibitors of sphingosine kinases, SKI (10 μM) or BT-190 (3 μM) recapitulated the same embryonic lethal phenotype.
source: Treatment with two chemical inhibitors of sphingosine kinases, SKI (10 μM) or BT-190 (3 μM) also recapitulated the same embryonic lethal phenotype (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is based on experimental treatment with sphingosine kinase inhibitors shown in Figure 2.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos given the same treatments do not fail epiboly and develop normally until they display later endoderm/cardiac defects.
source: In contrast, sphk2MZ embryos given the same treatments do not fail epiboly and (other than mild delay) develop normally (Figure 2I) until they display later endoderm/cardiac defects.
evidence: This is based on experimental treatment of sphk2MZ embryos shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Accumulation of sphingosine above a certain threshold is normally incompatible with embryonic development, yet tolerated in sphk2MZ mutant embryos.
source: Therefore, accumulation of sphingosine above a certain threshold is normally incompatible with embryonic development, yet tolerated in sphk2MZ mutant embryos.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing differential sensitivity to sphingosine.

claim: Embryos treated with 5 μM sphingosine, 3 μM BT-190, or 10 μM SKI show delayed progression with aggregation of thick F-actin positive bundles within the YCL.
source: Compared to control embryos, those embryos treated with 5 μM sphingosine, 3 μM BT-190, or 10 μM SKI when stained with phalloidin show delayed progression with aggregation of thick F-actin positive bundles within the YCL (Figure 3A–D) as well as accumulation of F-actin within the cytoplasm of the EVL cells (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is based on phalloidin staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: Embryos treated with 5 μM sphingosine, 3 μM BT-190, or 10 μM SKI show accumulation of F-actin within the cytoplasm of the EVL cells.
source: Compared to control embryos, those embryos treated with 5 μM sphingosine, 3 μM BT-190, or 10 μM SKI when stained with phalloidin show delayed progression with aggregation of thick F-actin positive bundles within the YCL (Figure 3A–D) as well as accumulation of F-actin within the cytoplasm of the EVL cells (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is based on phalloidin staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: Staining with α-tubulin revealed a massively thickened microtubule layer within the YSL in embryos treated with 5 μM sphingosine or 3 μM BT-190.
source: Staining with α-tubulin revealed a massively thickened microtubule layer within the YSL (as indicated by brackets, which also highlights the delayed progression of the EVL compared to deep layer cells) in embryos treated with (J) 5 μM sphingosine or (K) 3 μM BT-190 as well as (M,N) microtubule aggregation in certain areas of the YCL (denoted by asterisks) and other areas that are completely devoid of microtubules.
evidence: This is based on α-tubulin staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: Embryos treated with sphingosine or BT-190 show microtubule aggregation in certain areas of the YCL and other areas that are completely devoid of microtubules.
source: Staining with α-tubulin revealed a massively thickened microtubule layer within the YSL (as indicated by brackets, which also highlights the delayed progression of the EVL compared to deep layer cells) in embryos treated with (J) 5 μM sphingosine or (K) 3 μM BT-190 as well as (M,N) microtubule aggregation in certain areas of the YCL (denoted by asterisks) and other areas that are completely devoid of microtubules.
evidence: This is based on α-tubulin staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: E-cadherin staining shows reduced localization at EVL cell membrane junctions and accumulation of staining within the EVL cytoplasm in embryos treated with 5 μM sphingosine or 3 μM BT-190.
source: E-cadherin staining shows reduced localization at EVL cell membrane junctions and accumulation of staining within the EVL cytoplasm in embryos treated with 5 μM sphingosine or 3 μM BT-190, compared to DMSO-treated control embryos (Figure 3O–Q).
evidence: This is based on E-cadherin staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos might regulate one or more genes encoding enzymes responsible for the biosynthesis of sphingosine from ceramide (ceramidases) or conversion of sphingosine into ceramide (ceramide synthase).
source: We hypothesized that sphk2MZ embryos might regulate one or more genes encoding enzymes responsible for the biosynthesis of sphingosine from ceramide (ceramidases) or conversion of sphingosine into ceramide (ceramide synthase).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Analysis showed only one gene, cers2b, that is significantly and strikingly upregulated in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype embryos.
source: Therefore we examined expression levels for all the ceramide synthase and ceramidase genes that are annotated in the zebrafish genome (some of which are duplicated). This analysis showed only one gene, cers2b, that is significantly and strikingly upregulated in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype embryos (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: sphk2MZ embryos up-regulate a salvage pathway for sphingosine turnover through a specific ceramide synthase gene, cers2b, which could potentially protect these embryos from sphingosine-mediated gastrulation defects.
source: This suggests that sphk2MZ embryos up-regulate a salvage pathway for sphingosine turnover through a specific ceramide synthase gene, cers2b, which could potentially protect these embryos from sphingosine-mediated gastrulation defects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing cers2b upregulation.

claim: Injection of cers2b MO into sphk2MZ embryos resulted in a phenocopy of the sphingosine-induced toxicity defect during early gastrulation in 60/288 (21%) embryos from four independent experiments.
source: Injection of the same amount of cers2b MO into sphk2MZ embryos resulted in a phenocopy of the sphingosine-induced toxicity defect during early gastrulation in 60/288 (21%) embryos from four independent experiments, with failure of epiboly and pinching of the blastoderm from the yolk cell (Figure 4B,C, p=0.015).
evidence: This is based on morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transcriptional up-regulation of cers2b is important for sphk2MZ embryos to resist the buildup of excessive sphingosine and complete epiboly.
source: This suggests that transcriptional up-regulation of cers2b is important for sphk2MZ embryos to resist the buildup of excessive sphingosine and complete epiboly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morpholino knockdown data.

claim: A line of fish carrying a 23 bp deletion in exon6 of the cers2b gene was established that is predicted to delete most of the Lag domain and generate a frame-shift with a premature stop codon.
source: We established a line of fish carrying a 23 bp deletion in exon6 of the cers2b gene that is predicted to delete most of the Lag domain and generate a frame-shift with a premature stop codon and a truncated protein that would lack enzymatic function.
evidence: This describes the generation of a cers2b mutant line using CRISPR.

claim: When sphk2MZ; cers2b+/- adult fish were crossed to each other, the resulting clutches consistently had approximately 25% of the embryos that phenocopied the gastrulation defect caused by treating wildtype embryos with excess sphingosine.
source: When crossed to each other, the resulting clutches consistently had approximately 25% of the embryos that phenocopied the gastrulation defect caused by treating wildtype embryos with excess sphingosine (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The cers2b gene fails to be up-regulated in the sphk2 morphants.
source: We note that the cers2b gene fails to be up-regulated in the sphk2 morphants (Figure 4E), and neither do these embryos show increased ceramide levels (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: sphk2 morphants do not show increased ceramide levels.
source: We note that the cers2b gene fails to be up-regulated in the sphk2 morphants (Figure 4E), and neither do these embryos show increased ceramide levels (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Wildtype embryos treated with sphingosine fail to activate expression of cers2b.
source: Likewise, wildtype embryos treated with sphingosine fail to activate expression of cers2b (Figure 4G) or to significantly increase levels of total ceramides (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Wildtype embryos treated with sphingosine do not significantly increase levels of total ceramides.
source: Likewise, wildtype embryos treated with sphingosine fail to activate expression of cers2b (Figure 4G) or to significantly increase levels of total ceramides (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The increased sphingosine level associated with transcriptional activation of cers2b is dependent on the maternal loss of Sphk2 function.
source: Therefore, the data suggest that the increased sphingosine level associated with transcriptional activation of cers2b is dependent on the maternal loss of Sphk2 function, and neither wildtype embryos nor morphants are able to respond to increased sphingosine levels by up-regulation of the cers2b gene.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data comparing maternal-zygotic mutants, morphants, and wildtype embryos.

claim: Neither wildtype embryos nor morphants are able to respond to increased sphingosine levels by up-regulation of the cers2b gene.
source: Therefore, the data suggest that the increased sphingosine level associated with transcriptional activation of cers2b is dependent on the maternal loss of Sphk2 function, and neither wildtype embryos nor morphants are able to respond to increased sphingosine levels by up-regulation of the cers2b gene.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The ratio between firefly luciferase to renilla luciferase (FL/RL) was 9-fold higher in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype embryos.
source: In three independent experiments using a total of 114 embryos of each genotype per experiment (n = 38 samples, each sample comprised from three embryos) the ratio between firefly luciferase to renilla luciferase (FL/RL) was 9-fold higher in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype embryos (Figure 5A, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Key regulatory regions conferring both promoter activity and enhanced response in sphk2MZ mutant embryos are present in the 400 bp region at the 5' end of the 1.7 kb promoter construct.
source: These results indicate that key regulatory regions conferring both promoter activity and enhanced response in sphk2MZ mutant embryos are present in the 400 bp region at the 5' end of the 1.7 kb promoter construct.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the promoter deletion analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When the 400 bp fragment was cloned upstream of an independent minimal SV40 promoter, the resulting construct fully recapitulates a 9-fold enhanced activity in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype.
source: Indeed, when this 400 bp fragment was cloned upstream of an independent minimal SV40 promoter, although the basal activity was somewhat lower, the resulting construct fully recapitulates a 9-fold enhanced activity in sphk2MZ embryos compared to wildtype (Figures 5A and 400 bp).
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of Cers2b consistently and significantly decreased expression of the cers2b:luciferase reporter.
source: Expression of Cers2b consistently and significantly decreased expression of the cers2b:luciferase reporter (Figure 5B), indicating that Cer2b can be a functional repressor of its own gene.
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays in HEK293T cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cers2b can be a functional repressor of its own gene.
source: Expression of Cers2b consistently and significantly decreased expression of the cers2b:luciferase reporter (Figure 5B), indicating that Cer2b can be a functional repressor of its own gene.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the luciferase reporter data.

claim: Addition of 10 μM sphingosine to the transfected cells relieved the repressor activity of Cers2b so that the reporter was expressed at levels not significantly different from the control conditions without Cers2b.
source: Addition of 10 μM sphingosine to the transfected cells relieved this repressor activity so that the reporter was expressed at levels not significantly different from the control conditions without Cers2b.
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A two amino acid mutation (R121W, R122S) in the Cers2b coding sequence is predicted to impair the conserved structure of the homeodomain.
source: To test if this activity was dependent on the homeobox domain, a two amino acid mutation was introduced into the Cers2b coding sequence (R121W, R122S), which is predicted to impair the conserved structure of the homeodomain (Banerjee-Basu and Baxevanis, 2001).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous literature about homeodomain structure.

claim: The RR121-122WS alteration eliminated the capacity for Cers2b to repress its own promoter.
source: Like addition of sphingosine, the RR121-122WS alteration eliminated the capacity for Cers2b to repress its own promoter (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Lag-mutant protein retains the ability to repress the reporter controlled by the cers2b promoter.
source: As shown Figure 5B, The Lag-mutant protein retains the ability to repress the reporter controlled by the cers2b promoter.
evidence: This is based on luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Lag-mutant protein fails to generate ceramide above background levels.
source: Compared to the wildtype protein, the Lag-mutant fails to generate ceramide above background levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on ceramide measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The HOX mutant protein retains the ability, equivalent to the wildtype protein, to increase ceramide levels, but is unable to repress activity of the promoter.
source: In contrast, the HOX mutant protein retains the ability, equivalent to the wildtype protein, to increase ceramide levels, but is unable to repress activity of the promoter.
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The HOX domain is required for cers2 gene regulation, independent of enzymatic function.
source: Therefore, the HOX domain is required for cers2 gene regulation, independent of enzymatic function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mutational analysis data.

claim: Cers2-GFP protein is localized primarily to the ER, throughout the cell including contiguous to the nuclear membrane.
source: As expected, Cers2-GFP protein is localized primarily to the ER, throughout the cell including contiguous to the nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Following exposure to 10 μM sphingosine, there is a considerable change in the distribution of the Cers2-GFP fusion protein and notably enhanced signal associated with the nuclear membrane.
source: Following exposure to 10 μM sphingosine, a condition that leads to de-repression of the reporter that is regulated by the cers2b promoter, there is a considerable change in the distribution of the fusion protein and notably enhanced signal associated with the nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was a marked enrichment for Cers2b in the nuclear fraction following exposure to sphingosine.
source: In this case there was a marked enrichment for Cers2b in the nuclear fraction following exposure to sphingosine (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on western blotting of subcellular fractions shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Sphingosine induction caused Cers2b association primarily with nuclear membranes.
source: However, when the nuclear fraction was further separated, we found that sphingosine induction caused Cers2b association primarily with nuclear membranes (Figure 6C), consistent with the confocal imaging.
evidence: This is based on nuclear membrane fractionation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: It appears more likely that Cers2b impacts promoter activity by an indirect mechanism, perhaps acting at the nuclear membrane to process nuclear sphingosine.
source: Therefore, we did not find evidence that Cers2 functions as a nuclear protein and while function as a transcription factor can't be ruled out, it appears more likely that Cers2b impacts promoter activity by an indirect mechanism, perhaps acting at the nuclear membrane to process nuclear sphingosine.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the localization data.

claim: Lipidomics comparing wildtype and sphk2 mutant oocytes confirmed a lack of S1P and relatively higher levels of sphingosine in the mutant oocytes.
source: Lipidomics comparing wildtype and sphk2 mutant oocytes confirmed, similar to the sphk2MZ embryos, a lack of S1P and relatively higher levels of sphingosine in the mutant oocytes (Figure 7A), although in this case the total ceramide levels were not significantly different (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic profiling of oocytes shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Total ceramide levels were not significantly different between wildtype and sphk2 mutant oocytes.
source: Lipidomics comparing wildtype and sphk2 mutant oocytes confirmed, similar to the sphk2MZ embryos, a lack of S1P and relatively higher levels of sphingosine in the mutant oocytes (Figure 7A), although in this case the total ceramide levels were not significantly different (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic profiling of oocytes shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In situ hybridization experiments confirmed strikingly higher levels of cers2b transcripts in the mutant oocytes compared to wildtype.
source: We also carried out in situ hybridization experiments probing oocytes derived from ovaries of sphk2 mutant females. This confirmed strikingly higher levels of cers2b transcripts in the mutant oocytes compared to wildtype (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Early embryos derived from a sphk2 null female are resistant to rupture when exposed to exogenous sphingosine, despite a functional sphk2 allele inherited from the wildtype male.
source: Furthermore, early embryos derived from a sphk2 null female are resistant to rupture when exposed to exogenous sphingosine, despite a functional sphk2 allele inherited from the wildtype male (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on experimental treatment of embryos shown in Figure 7D.

claim: All the data are fully consistent with a sphingosine-induced Cers2b-based protective mechanism during oogenesis.
source: All the data are fully consistent with a sphingosine-induced Cers2b-based protective mechanism during oogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the oocyte data.

claim: Previous studies confirmed that Sphk2 is an enzyme required to generate S1P used during early embryogenesis in an S1P receptor-dependent manner to regulate endoderm convergence and heart tube formation.
source: Previous studies confirmed that Sphk2 is an enzyme required to generate S1P used during early embryogenesis in an S1P receptor-dependent manner to regulate endoderm convergence and heart tube formation (Hisano et al., 2015a; Mendelson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The sphk2MZ mutant embryos have increased sphingosine levels due to the failure to convert this substrate to S1P.
source: The sphk2MZ mutant embryos have increased sphingosine levels due to the failure to convert this substrate to S1P.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lipidomic data.

claim: The mutant embryos are nevertheless relatively resistant to toxicity caused by excess sphingosine.
source: Even with the increased sphingosine levels, the mutant embryos are nevertheless relatively resistant to toxicity caused by excess sphingosine.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing differential sensitivity to sphingosine.

claim: The mutant embryos have engaged an alternative program to convert sphingosine to a non-toxic metabolite.
source: This indicates that they have engaged an alternative program to convert sphingosine to a non-toxic metabolite.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the resistance to sphingosine toxicity.

claim: The reason that Sphk2MZ embryos are delayed in epiboly is not known, but it is speculated to be caused by destabilization of the actin-microtubule cytoskeletal network due to accumulation of excess sphingosine.
source: The reason that Sphk2MZ embryos are delayed in epiboly is not known, but we speculate that it is caused by destabilization of the actin-microtubule cytoskeletal network due to accumulation of excess sphingosine.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the developmental delay.

claim: Upregulation of cers2b in the mutant embryos manages to maintain sphingosine levels below the 'catastrophic' threshold.
source: Upregulation of cers2b in the mutant embryos manages to maintain sphingosine levels below this 'catastrophic' threshold, generating a phenotype similar to wildtype embryos treated with the 3 μM lower dose.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: A good candidate for mediating the connection to cytoskeleton is the p21-activated kinase Pak1.
source: A good candidate for mediating the connection to cytoskeleton is the p21-activated kinase Pak1.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on known functions of Pak1.

claim: Pak kinases can localize to cortical actin structures, and expression of activated mutants induces cytoskeletal reorganization, including loss of actin stress fibers.
source: Pak kinases can localize to cortical actin structures, and expression of activated mutants induces cytoskeletal reorganization, including loss of actin stress fibers (Manser et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pak1 signaling is implicated during epiboly in sustaining E-cadherin at adherens junctions.
source: Pak1 signaling is also implicated during epiboly in sustaining E-cadherin at adherens junctions (Tay et al., 2010), which also fails in the sphingosine-treated embryos.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sphingosine was shown previously to activate PAK1 in mammalian cells in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, sphingosine was shown previously to activate PAK1 in mammalian cells in a concentration-dependent manner (Bokoch et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The dramatic blastoderm constriction phenotype is remarkably similar to the maternal-zygotic betty boop (bbp) mutant embryo.
source: The dramatic blastoderm constriction phenotype is remarkably similar to the maternal-zygotic betty boop (bbp) mutant embryo (Holloway et al., 2009), suggesting that it could also involve defects in a p38/MAPKAPK2 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: It has long been recognized that while Sphk1 is localized primarily in the cytoplasm, Sphk2 is mostly a nuclear protein.
source: On the other hand, it has long been recognized that while Sphk1 is localized primarily in the cytoplasm, Sphk2 is mostly a nuclear protein, and may be particularly important for regulating nuclear sphingosine levels, which could impact DNA synthesis (Igarashi et al., 2003) or oxidative stress otherwise leading to DNA damage and apoptosis (Van Brocklyn and Williams, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sphk2 may be particularly important for regulating nuclear sphingosine levels, which could impact DNA synthesis or oxidative stress otherwise leading to DNA damage and apoptosis.
source: On the other hand, it has long been recognized that while Sphk1 is localized primarily in the cytoplasm, Sphk2 is mostly a nuclear protein, and may be particularly important for regulating nuclear sphingosine levels, which could impact DNA synthesis (Igarashi et al., 2003) or oxidative stress otherwise leading to DNA damage and apoptosis (Van Brocklyn and Williams, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: sphk2 is expressed as a maternal transcript, and this is also true of cers2b in the sphk2MZ mutant embryos.
source: We note that sphk2 is expressed as a maternal transcript, and this is also true of cers2b in the sphk2MZ mutant embryos.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing maternal expression.

claim: The genome might be especially vigilant at limiting nuclear sphingosine levels during oogenesis in order to protect genomic integrity.
source: This suggests that the genome might be especially vigilant at limiting nuclear sphingosine levels during oogenesis in order to protect genomic integrity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the maternal expression pattern.

claim: Previous studies showed that sphingolipids, particularly S1P, were shown to protect oocytes from apoptosis induced by genotoxic stress or chemotherapy in mice and primates.
source: In this context, it is of interest to note previous studies where sphingolipids, particularly S1P, were shown to protect oocytes from apoptosis induced by genotoxic stress or chemotherapy in mice and primates (Morita et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: S1P treatment in vitro was shown to induce oocyte survival.
source: S1P treatment in vitro was shown to induce oocyte survival (Hannoun et al., 2010), and acid ceramidase is known to modulate oocyte apoptosis (Eliyahu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Acid ceramidase is known to modulate oocyte apoptosis.
source: S1P treatment in vitro was shown to induce oocyte survival (Hannoun et al., 2010), and acid ceramidase is known to modulate oocyte apoptosis (Eliyahu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The findings could have practical implications in reproductive sciences and in vitro fertilization technology.
source: Thus, our findings could have practical implications in reproductive sciences and in vitro fertilization technology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Cers2b contains a homeobox domain, required for repressing transcriptional activity of its own promoter.
source: It is interesting that Cers2b contains a homeobox domain, required for repressing transcriptional activity of its own promoter.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing the HOX domain is required for repression.

claim: Under conditions with limiting sphingosine levels the Cers2b enzyme functions to repress its own gene and thereby limit sphingosine conversion to ceramide.
source: This leads to a model whereby under conditions with limiting sphingosine levels the Cers2b enzyme functions to repress its own gene and thereby limit sphingosine conversion to ceramide (perhaps also favoring conversion to S1P).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: If sphingosine levels exceed a certain threshold, this is recognized by binding of sphingosine to the Lag domain of Cers2b, which relieves Cers2b repression activity and activates enzymatic activity to remove sphingosine by metabolism to ceramide.
source: If sphingosine levels exceed a certain threshold, for example by loss of Sphk2 activity and/or increased ceramidase activity, this is recognized by binding of sphingosine to the Lag domain of Cers2b, which relieves Cers2b repression activity, perhaps through a conformational alteration, and activates enzymatic activity to remove sphingosine by metabolism to ceramide.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: The cers2b transcript levels are markedly enhanced, at levels that are recapitulated by the promoter using a luciferase reporter with no shared RNA sequences.
source: However, we note that the cers2b transcript levels are markedly enhanced, at levels that are recapitulated by the promoter using a luciferase reporter with no shared RNA sequences.
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR and luciferase reporter data.

claim: The increase in cers2b is highly specific to the cers2b transcript.
source: Furthermore, the increase is highly specific to the cers2b transcript.
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR analysis of multiple ceramide synthase and ceramidase genes.

claim: 15 years ago Venkataraman and Futerman speculated whether the presence of a homeobox domain suggests that the enzymes might act as dual sphingosine sensors and transcriptional regulators, analogous to how sterol regulatory element binding protein (SREBP) senses and modulates sterols.
source: 15 years ago Venkataraman and Futerman speculated whether the presence of a homeobox domain suggests that the enzymes might act as dual sphingosine sensors and transcriptional regulators, analogous to how sterol regulatory element binding protein (SREBP) senses and modulates sterols (Venkataraman and Futerman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpressing mammalian Cers2 in HT29 colon cancer cells caused a modest but significant reduction in transcription of a reporter gene regulated by an acid ceramidase promoter.
source: Consistent with our results, overexpressing mammalian Cers2 in HT29 colon cancer cells caused a modest but significant reduction in transcription of a reporter gene regulated by an acid ceramidase promoter (Tirodkar et al., 2015), suggesting that Cers2 might have additional pathway-relevant targets.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cers2 might have additional pathway-relevant targets.
source: Consistent with our results, overexpressing mammalian Cers2 in HT29 colon cancer cells caused a modest but significant reduction in transcription of a reporter gene regulated by an acid ceramidase promoter (Tirodkar et al., 2015), suggesting that Cers2 might have additional pathway-relevant targets.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: The single Drosophila Cers ortholog, Schlank, also has a homeodomain, in addition to the Lag motif.
source: The single Drosophila Cers ortholog, Schlank, also has a homeodomain, in addition to the Lag motif.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila Cers ortholog.

claim: schlank mutants could be rescued by expression of variant proteins lacking a functional Lag motif, as long as they contained the homeodomain and a nuclear localization signal.
source: Interestingly, schlank mutants could be rescued by expression of variant proteins lacking a functional Lag motif, as long as they contained the homeodomain and a nuclear localization signal (Voelzmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The critical role played by this ER/nuclear membrane-localized enzyme is in autoregulation of sphingolipid metabolism.
source: While the mechanism for Cers2b action during zebrafish embryogenesis remains unclear, our results suggest the critical role played by this ER/nuclear membrane-localized enzyme is in autoregulation of sphingolipid metabolism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The data provide new evidence for a role of ceramide synthase in vertebrate embryonic development.
source: Our data provide new evidence for a role of ceramide synthase in vertebrate embryonic development, but the concept of a dual role in metabolism and transcription has been considered previously.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Cers2b may play a central role in coordinating a response following sensing of sphingosine levels to the transcriptional machinery in the regulation of sphingolipid metabolism.
source: In fact, together with our observations, it seems likely that Cers2b may play a central role in coordinating a response following sensing of sphingosine levels to the transcriptional machinery in the regulation of sphingolipid metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The observation linking Cers2b to genomic sensing/transcription was only made possible by close examination of subtle phenotypes in the sphk2MZ mutant embryo.
source: Our observation linking Cers2b to genomic sensing/transcription was only made possible by close examination of subtle phenotypes in the sphk2MZ mutant embryo.
evidence: This is a reflection on the experimental approach.

claim: The identical phenotype caused by excess sphingosine in wildtype embryos was also seen in sphk2 morphants.
source: The identical phenotype caused by excess sphingosine in wildtype embryos (pinching off of the blastoderm during epiboly and embryonic lethality) was also seen in sphk2 morphants.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of morphants.

claim: Mutants (but not morphants or wildtype embryos treated with sphingosine) are able to recognize the defect and have time to take corrective action through engaging the salvage Cers2 pathway.
source: This suggests that mutants (but not morphants or wildtype embryos treated with sphingosine) are able to recognize the defect and have time to take corrective action through engaging the salvage Cers2 pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential responses between mutants and morphants.

claim: The process of engaging the salvage Cers2 pathway apparently occurs during oogenesis, since it involves the expression of maternal transcripts.
source: The process apparently occurs during oogenesis, since it involves the expression of maternal transcripts.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the maternal expression of cers2b.

claim: The capacity of zebrafish embryos to compensate for mutant genes may be relatively robust.
source: The capacity of zebrafish embryos to compensate for mutant genes may be relatively robust (see also [Rossi et al., 2015]), and at least partially responsible for the reported disparity between mutant and morphant phenotypes (Kok et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The capacity of zebrafish embryos to compensate for mutant genes is at least partially responsible for the reported disparity between mutant and morphant phenotypes.
source: The capacity of zebrafish embryos to compensate for mutant genes may be relatively robust (see also [Rossi et al., 2015]), and at least partially responsible for the reported disparity between mutant and morphant phenotypes (Kok et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The capacity of zebrafish embryos to compensate for mutant genes can be fortuitous for revealing novel biological regulatory mechanisms.
source: It can also be fortuitous for revealing novel biological regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is a reflection on the implications of genetic compensation.
